Our method, DRAFT (Decoding and Reconstructing 3D room lAyouts from fMRI and Trajectories), extracts a compact layout representation from the early visual cortex and fuses this neural code with the geometric free space derived from camera motion. To evaluate it, we propose layout r, the Pearson correlation between predicted and ray-cast log depths. On ten held-out scenes (20 participants), DRAFT reaches a layout r of 0.480, outperforming the camera path alone (0.446) and seven fMRI decoders (at most 0.429). DRAFT also works as a plug-in that improves all seven decoders without retraining, raising their layout r from 0.171-0.429 to 0.487-0.493. Brain activity and camera motion can thus recover the metric layout of unseen rooms, a first step toward reconstructing the 3D spaces people see.

papers.title: Testing for peer effects in short panels without identifying the network structure
papers.authors: Tom Boot; Artūras Juodis
papers.abstract: We propose an instrument-based test for peer effects in short-T panels when the underlying network is unknown. The test avoids estimating the network by aggregating pairwise comparisons between covariate-projected outcomes of potential peers and residualized own outcomes. The statistic is designed for fixed-T, large-N settings with individual fixed effects, heterogeneous slopes, heteroskedasticity, and serial dependence within units. We also develop a weighted extension that accounts for additive common time effects. The limiting distribution is standard Gaussian when the norm of the projected component of the outcomes is bounded away from zero, but can be nonstandard when it is local to zero. We derive a conditional Gaussian limit experiment and a feasible conditional Monte Carlo procedure to obtain uniformly valid critical values. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the conditional procedure leads to accurate size control while retaining power against latent peer-effect alternatives.

papers.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
papers.authors: Fabian Isensee; Constantin Ulrich Harsy; Maximilian Rokuss; Benjamin Hamm; Philipp Vollmuth et al.
papers.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. Code: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nninteractive-agent

papers.title: Conditional Mean Flows for Frequency-Domain Scattered Wavefield Generation
papers.authors: Lipeng Lai; Shaohuan Zu
papers.abstract: Frequency-domain wavefield modeling underpins seismic imaging and inversion, where repeated Helmholtz solutions become costly as velocity models, source locations, and frequencies vary. Neural operators learn mappings between physical fields, and their accuracy can decline outside the training distribution. Diffusion models learn wavefield distributions and generally require repeated sampling evaluations to produce accurate fields. A conditional mean flows model is introduced for complex scattered-wavefield generation. The analytical background wavefield serves as a condition alongside the velocity model, supplying spatially organized information about the source location and frequency. Learning the scattered wavefield avoids the point-source singularity in the target and supports generalization across these physical conditions. The model estimates the average transport velocity over a finite interval connecting Gaussian noise to the scattered field. This representation captures the accumulated displacement and permits both full-interval one-step generation and interval-partitioned sampling. Trained on OpenFWI, the model is evaluated on in-distribution and out-of-distribution velocity structures, frequency generalization, and inference efficiency. In most evaluated settings, one-step mean flows sampling achieves lower wavefield error than multi-step diffusion. Because each sampling step requires another network evaluation, accurate one-step generation also reduces inference time. These results indicate that mean flows can provide accurate and efficient frequency-domain scattered-wavefield generation.

papers.title: Tilt-Rotor Quadcopter with Learned Residual Control and Mode-Dependent State Estimation
papers.authors: Ninad Joshi; Prabhat Kumar
papers.abstract: Tilt-rotor quadcopters redirect thrust for translation without banking, but complicate modeling, state estimation, and disturbance rejection. This paper presents a simulation-based flight stack for a \SI{2.00}{\kilo\gram} tilt-rotor quadcopter. The system uses a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model with first-order motor dynamics and two-axis rotor tilt, parameterized using a 3D CAD model. A cascaded PD controller commands forward and lateral tilt angles. A 14-state EKF fuses sensor data across hover, early-transition, and transition modes using a hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) classifier to prevent covariance discontinuities. Because the proportional position loop leaves a steady-state offset under constant wind, a small bounded neural residual is added on top of the unmodified PD controller. It is trained by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged access to the true wind, while the deployed network never observes wind. In simulation, the EKF achieves a post-settling position root mean square error (RMSE) of \SI{0.226}{\metre} (horizontal) and \SI{0.03}{\metre} (vertical) and an attitude RMSE below \SI{0.8}{\degree}, and it estimates a wind velocity of $(\num{2.0}, \num{-1.2})\,\unit{\metre\per\second}$ to within \SI{0.15}{\metre\per\second} per axis. The residual reduces steady-state station-keeping error under wind by approximately \SI{49}{\percent}, from \SI{0.117}{\metre} to \SI{0.060}{\metre} at \SI{1.5}{\metre\per\second} and from \SI{0.319}{\metre} to \SI{0.162}{\metre} at an out-of-distribution \SI{3.9}{\metre\per\second}. The framework provides a basis for hardware-in-the-loop and flight-test studies.

papers.title: Contact Renormalization of One-Mode Electron Correlation: Validation in Four- and Ten-Electron Systems
papers.authors: Itai Panas
papers.abstract: A stationary many-electron eigenstate has one dynamical phase although its internal response can be strongly multimode. We ask whether the stationary Hartree--Fock information carrier contains enough information to determine the scalar correlation energy through one effective return. In regularized Hartree--Fock, Gaussian primitive products fix a minimum-information relative-coordinate mode before any one-mode reduction; virial completion defines the correlation source, while exact contact measures the additional return restriction created by neighboring occupied pairs. The Be-like $1s^22s^2$ sequence establishes the one-valence-pair boundary: with no neighboring occupied valence pair, the source returns through the universal floor $D_0=\sqrt{1+δ^2}$. Ten-electron molecules and Ne-like ions then test how finite-pair contact dresses that return. The same parameter-free source--return construction reproduces the established molecular and ionic correlation trends with quantitative accuracy. The numerical agreement therefore serves as validation of a physical separation between source strength and return restriction, rather than as the objective by itself.

papers.title: Bayes Factor Testing of Linear and Nonlinear Effects in Additive Gaussian Process Regression
papers.authors: Yueheng Wu; Joran Jongerling; Joris Mulder
papers.abstract: Gaussian process regression flexibly models nonlinear relationships between predictors and an outcome variable. A central question in this modeling framework is whether each predictor affects the outcome linearly, nonlinearly, or not at all. We propose a Bayesian testing framework for this problem within additive Gaussian process regression. Each predictor is decomposed into a standardized linear component with a $g$-prior and an orthogonalized Gaussian process component capturing nonlinear structure. The latter is governed by a standardized magnitude parameter whose value zero removes the component. Local and non-local priors are considered for the standardized magnitude parameter. Bayes factors for testing the linear and nonlinear effects are computed from the fitted full model via Savage-Dickey-type identities, avoiding expensive marginal likelihood computations of many different models. To assess the accuracy of the Bayes factor estimates, the outcomes are compared to bridge sampling estimates. Simulations and empirical applications show the performance and applicability of the methodology.

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of 3D-Printed Freeform Waveguides with a Transformation Optics-Based Beam Propagation Method
papers.authors: Sina Foroutan-Barenji; Jonas Krimmer; Stefan Singer; Christian Koos; Wolfgang Freude
papers.abstract: An efficient numerical method is introduced for simulating wave propagation in 3D-printed freeform waveguides, referred to as photonic wire bonds (PWBs). This approach integrates transformation optics (TO) with curvilinear meshing to map the original 3D freeform PWB structure onto a straight waveguide, which possesses anisotropic material characteristics. The resulting waveguide is then analyzed using an anisotropic full-vectorial beam propagation method (BPM). To validate the performance and effectiveness of the proposed TO-BPM algorithm, a comparison is made with the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) technique. Our approach reduces the simulation time by more than two orders of magnitude, depending on the degree of trajectory bending, in combination with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 3.9% in power transmission simulation relative to the FDTD.

papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
papers.authors: Jialin Tian; Zhuofan Li; Xinkai Wang; Bokai Lin; Chenyi Wang et al.
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
papers.authors: Ignacy Kolton; Wenxuan Li; Zongwei Zhou; Jarosław B. Ćwikła; Arkadiusz Sitek et al.
papers.abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.

papers.title: Bound-Conditioned Latent Inference for Progressive Image Compression
papers.authors: Jaeseok Jang; Seungmin Jeon; Kwang Pyo Choi; Chang-Su Kim
papers.abstract: Progressive image compression reconstructs images from prefixes of a single bitstream and therefore involves sequential latent inference under partial observations. Existing trit-plane codecs mainly treat decoded trits as discrete symbols for probability prediction, without fully exploiting their role as interval constraints on the underlying continuous latents. We propose bound-conditioned latent inference (BLI), a framework that reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints. At each coding step, the trits decoded so far define lower and upper bounds for each latent element. BLI uses the center and width of these bounds, together with hyperprior information shared by the encoder and decoder, to jointly refine the Gaussian parameters $(μ,σ)$ for entropy modeling and the latent estimate $\hat{y}$ for reconstruction. As additional trits are decoded, the feasible intervals shrink monotonically, yielding tighter constraints for the next inference step and enabling flexible in-plane refinement schedules. Experiments on Kodak, CLIC, and JPEG-AI show that BLI achieves state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among progressive image codecs, reducing BD-rate by $17.78\%$ over DPICT and by $7.96\%$ over CTC on Kodak, while replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about $5.3\times$ fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC.

papers.title: Ground-Truth-First Benchmarking of Reinforcement Learning via Converse Optimality: From Smooth, Fully Observed Systems to Non-Smooth or Partially Observed Tasks
papers.authors: Grégoire Ouerdane; Sinan Ibrahim; Stefan Streif; Pavel Osinenko
papers.abstract: Benchmarking in reinforcement learning is usually relative: algorithms are ranked by returns on environments with unknown optima. Distance to optimality remains unobservable, while conclusions may depend on reward design, stochasticity, hyperparameters, environment selection, and simulator details. We develop a ground-truth-first framework based on converse optimality, constructing each task with a certified optimal value function and policy withheld from learners and used only for evaluation. The framework unifies two modes: sensitivity benchmarking samples certified environments from continuous-time generators to assess robustness to task variation, while oracle-referenced comparison uses native discrete-time generators to evaluate policies via optimality gap, regret, and policy error. Continuous-time models support physically interpretable sensitivity studies but introduce dependence on the simulator step ($Δt$) and numerical scheme. Native discrete-time models align the environment, oracle, and learner on the same transition law, eliminating external integration choices as a confounder. We reproduce quantitative results covering optimizer sensitivity and oracle-referenced comparisons on serial planar arms, dynamically extended nonholonomic vehicles, and quadrotor-inspired tasks. The methodology extends beyond smooth affine Gaussian systems: virtual-input pullback handles non-affine raw-action interfaces and finite-covariance non-Gaussian disturbances. A non-smooth converse optimality formulation enables certified benchmarks with kinked value functions and switching surfaces. For partially observed evaluation, an information-state formulation reduces benchmarking to converse optimality on a sufficient statistic and provides an information-penalty reference. Code, fixtures, and diagnostics are available on the public project page.

papers.title: LieGROG: A Lie algebra approach for calibrating GRAPPA operators
papers.authors: Tobias Wech
papers.abstract: Purpose: In multi-coil acquisitions based on non-Cartesian k-space sampling, image reconstruction using GRAPPA Operator based gridding (GROG) can provide advantages with respect to the non-uniform FFT (NUFFT): It waives both the need for calculating a density compensation function, and for transferring back and forth between Cartesian and non-Cartesian points in iterative algorithms. Non-trivial noise propagation and self-calibration limited to specific trajectories, however, have contributed to GROG being rather sparsely applied so far.   Theory and Methods: The group structure of the GRAPPA Operator allows estimating its generator as a single joint fit for all k-space dimensions within the associated Lie algebra. Assuming a linear regime, the generator can be fitted using subsequent pairs of sampling points from nearly any arbitrary non-Cartesian read-out. This approach called LieGROG was evaluated against classical GROG calibration and NUFFT/Toeplitz, using simulations with an analytic ground truth and various 2D and 3D MR-scans employing typical non-Cartesian trajectories.   Results: Throughout all applications, LieGROG proved to provide fast, robust and straightforward calibration of the GRAPPA Operator. It clearly outperformed the classical GROG calibration approaches in terms of noise amplification. LieGROG matched the results of the NUFFT/Toeplitz-based reference MR reconstructions closely, while being 6 to 189 times faster and reducing peak VRAM by 20 to 45% in the 3D experiments.   Conclusion: LieGROG transforms GROG into a more versatile and stable tool, ultimately aligning non-Cartesian imaging with the standard, FFT-based reconstruction pipelines established for Cartesian scans.

papers.title: TwinStore: A Synthetic Consumer Platform Using Vision--Language Models
papers.authors: Minhyeok Lee
papers.abstract: We present TwinStore, a source-available synthetic consumer platform for physical retail built on vision--language models. TwinStore turns a store into a digital twin---from 82 ready-made formats, a floor-plan image or phone photos of its shelves---and fills it with synthetic shoppers who plan a trip, walk the aisles and decide what to buy by looking at rendered shelves with packs, price tags and promotion signs. Every trip ends in a receipt, so a layout, price, pack or promotion can be tried on the same shoppers before it reaches the store. Around this core, TwinStore provides 3D playback, paired comparisons and layout optimization, shopper interviews, a trade-area model, counterfactual edits of real shelf photos, a marketing studio with eleven tools, and an assistant that turns a plain sentence into a drafted study or an answer grounded in a run's own numbers. In a held-out validation on eleven public datasets, simulated receipts approach the households' own natural variation (category-mix divergence 0.017--0.018 against a real drift of 0.012), price elasticities fall inside the range measured in the field, and three independent decision models agree. TwinStore runs on cloud or on-device models and is distributed with installers for Windows, macOS and Linux.

papers.title: Query-Time Calibration of CLIP Features for Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
papers.authors: Dominik Engel; Yousef Rajeh; Leon Sick; Ivan Viola
papers.abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.

papers.title: Silicon Samples Match the Answers but Not the Respondents
papers.authors: Yusuke Kumagae; Masahiro Kaneko
papers.abstract: Silicon sampling generates survey respondents by having a large language model (LLM) answer a survey as a person with given demographic attributes, and the resulting synthetic populations are increasingly used in place of human ones. Existing evaluations focus on individual-answer accuracy, per-question answer distributions, and correlations across questions. None of these compares the respondents themselves, so a generator whose respondents have combinations of answers found in no human respondent can still score well if it reproduces every answer distribution. We propose the respondent coverage gap (RCG), which represents each respondent as a point defined by their complete answer profile and measures how far each human respondent is from the nearest generated one, relative to the distance between human samples. On two US social surveys, all six LLMs we evaluate leave human respondents uncovered, and under our main settings, they fall behind a baseline that samples each answer independently from the human marginals. Across the prompting and inference settings we test, every LLM has a higher RCG than a Gaussian copula fitted to the human data.

papers.title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
papers.authors: Ying Li; Sanyou Wu; Zi Yang; Qiaochu Xu; Yuhao Liu et al.
papers.abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

papers.title: Strong uniqueness for fractional stochastic differential equations with sign drift
papers.authors: Ercan Sönmez; Yuliya Mishura
papers.abstract: Establishing pathwise uniqueness for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$ remains challenging, particularly for discontinuous drifts beyond the regularity regimes of existing theories. A canonical example is the sign drift, for which uniqueness fails in the corresponding deterministic equation. In this paper, we complement recent strong existence results by establishing pathwise uniqueness for the equation with sign drift perturbed by fractional Brownian motion for every $H\in(1/2,1)$, thus obtaining strong well-posedness. Our proof develops a new approach based on the infinite iteration of an inequality arising from a fixed-point relation, combined with tail probability estimates exploiting the Gaussian structure of the noise. The methods and results cover a broader class of Gaussian Volterra processes satisfying suitable local nondeterminism and positivity conditions.

papers.title: Surface Defects in the $\mathcal{N}=2$ Lens Space Index and Elliptic Integrability
papers.authors: Masahito Yamazaki
papers.abstract: We determine the surface-defect difference operators of the 4d $\mathcal{N}=2$ lens space index for class $\mathcal{S}$ theories of type $A_{N-1}$ on $(\mathbb{S}^3/\mathbb{Z}_r)\times\mathbb{S}^1$. For generic fugacities $(p,q,t)$ and arbitrary rank $N$, orbifold order $r$ and discrete holonomies, their coefficients are finite products of theta functions with nomes $p^r$ and $q^r$. After an explicit gauge transformation, Gaussian in the holonomies, each operator factorizes into two elliptic Ruijsenaars--Schneider-type operators with step $pq$, one with nome $p^r$ and one with nome $q^r$, acting on variables glued along a lattice. Using this factorization and a Wronski-type relation, we prove that all the operators commute. We also establish a sufficient criterion for self-adjointness with respect to the bilinear vector multiplet pairing. It applies to the basic mixed operator and, in suitable parameter chambers, to the pure $p$- and $q$-type operators; for general mixed operators the contour prescription remains open. These results support the expectations from S-duality.

papers.title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
papers.authors: Chuanlin Zuo; Miloš Prágr; Arun Kumar Singh; Mohammad Loni; Reza Ghabcheloo
papers.abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.

papers.title: Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks: Enhancing Flexibility in Node Dependencies via penalized B-Splines
papers.authors: Aitor Oviedo-Madrid; Mabel Morales-Otero; Jose Gonzalez-Gomariz; Ruben Armañanzas
papers.abstract: Bayesian networks for continuous variables often rely on restrictive assumptions: linear Gaussian models lack flexibility to capture nonlinear dependencies, while non-parametric approaches provide greater flexibility at a high computational cost. This creates a gap for modeling scenarios where variables are approximately Gaussian but exhibit nonlinear relationships. We introduce Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks (SLGBN), a novel class of continuous Bayesian networks designed to bridge this gap, preserving Gaussian conditional distributions while introducing nonlinear conditional mean functions. The proposed framework provides a unified probabilistic framework combining linear Gaussian and nonlinear Gaussian conditional models within the same Bayesian network Nonlinear conditional mean functions are estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with penalized B-splines. We present parameter estimation procedures for both types of nodes, as well as a greedy hill-climbing algorithm for learning the network structure under the SLGBN framework. To assess its performance, we compare SLGBN with other continuous Bayesian network models, including semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBN) and Linear Gaussian Bayesian networks (LGBN). Experimental results evaluate both goodness of fit and the ability to recover the underlying network structure. The results show that, in the presence of nonlinear Gaussian relationships, SLGBN achieves better fit and improved structure recovery compared to alternative models, particularly when combined with the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC*) score. Furthermore, by retaining Gaussian conditional distributions, SLGBN offers computational advantages over fully semiparametric approaches.

papers.title: Central limit theorem for the Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation
papers.authors: Yun Li; Longjie Xie; Li Yang; Qianning Zhang
papers.abstract: We establish the central limit theorem (CLT) for Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation of Langevin equations with state-dependent, possibly non-symmetric friction and multiplicative noise. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such result, even in the case of constant friction and additive noise. The result differs in an essential way from classical averaging CLTs and reveals a new two-scale fluctuation phenomenon. The normalized difference process retains a persistent fast component and is generally not tight in $C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$, thus the usual continuous-path CLT cannot hold. We derive an exact decomposition of the normalized difference into an accumulated slow fluctuation and a rapidly relaxing velocity correction. The auxiliary slow fluctuation converges to a linear diffusion driven by both the original Brownian motion and an additional independent Brownian noise whose effective covariance is characterized explicitly through a quadratic Poisson corrector. For every fixed $t>0$, the fast correction converges conditionally to its local Gaussian equilibrium. Consequently, the fixed-time fluctuation limit is identified as a Gaussian mixture: $$ \frac{\bar X_t-X_t^\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}} \Longrightarrow \bar Y_t+N^{1/2}(\bar X_t)ξ, $$ where $\bar X_t$ is the overdamped limit, $\bar Y_t$ is the limiting slow fluctuation, $N$ is the covariance of the terminal velocity correction and solves a Lyapunov equation, and $ξ$ is a standard Gaussian random variable independent of $(\bar X_t,\bar Y_t)$. A quantitative convergence rate is also provided. The result fills the remaining gap in the asymptotic theory of the overdamped approximation at the central limit scale, complementing the existing law of large numbers, moderate deviation and large deviation results.

papers.title: Distinct stellar-parameter dependencies of granulation and mesogranulation in red giants
papers.authors: Anohita Mallick; Jharnesh Verma; Shatanik Bhattacharya; Shravan M Hanasoge
papers.abstract: Granulation and mesogranulation represent different spatial and temporal scales of convection, but are commonly assumed to follow the same stellar atmospheric scaling relations in red giants. We test this assumption using the largest sample assembled for this purpose to date -- 9,328 Kepler red giants spanning the red giant branch and red clump phase, cross-matched with APOGEE stellar parameters. We model each star's power spectrum background to obtain the radius-corrected amplitude and characteristic frequency of both components, and derive empirical scaling relations with effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity through Bayesian model comparison. Gaussian Process and symbolic regression provide independent validation. We find that granulation and mesogranulation are not self-similar: their surface-gravity dependencies are statistically indistinguishable, consistent with a shared envelope geometry, but their temperature dependencies diverge: mesogranulation's amplitude rises steeply with Teff, whereas granulation's shows no statistically justified dependence, and both frequencies respond weakly and similarly. We propose that this pattern is consistent with granulation forming in a thin near-surface layer, where radiation takes over from convection and the Mach number depends only weakly on Teff. Mesogranulation originates deeper, where convection carries the full flux and its Mach number and cell size increase with Teff. Metallicity raises both amplitudes but has little effect on the frequencies. Our results indicate that the self-similarity assumption underlying two-component background models does not hold, with direct implications for background modeling and its downstream application in Galactic archaeology.

papers.title: Schatten limits for semi-commutators in Toeplitz quantization on Fock space
papers.authors: Jie Qin
papers.abstract: We solve a problem posed by Hu and Virtanen by characterizing, for every $0<p<\infty$, the bounded symbols $f$ for which $T_f^{(t)}T_g^{(t)}-T_{fg}^{(t)}$ tends to zero in the unnormalized Schatten $p$-norm or quasi-norm as $t\to0^+$ for every fixed bounded $g$. The setting is weighted Fock spaces over $\mathbb C^n$ with weights whose real Hessians are uniformly positive and bounded. Only constants satisfy the limit when $p<2n$; at $p=2n$, it is equivalent to the weak real gradient belonging to $L^{2n}(\mathbb R^{2n})$. When $p>2n$, the limit is characterized by relative weak compactness in $L^1(\mathbb R^{2n})$ of normalized local mean oscillation densities. For $p\ge2$, uniform convergence over $\|g\|_\infty\le1$ is equivalent to vanishing density mass. A continuous compactly supported counterexample for $p>2n$ shows that bounded density mass and convergence for $g=\bar f$ do not imply convergence for every fixed bounded $g$. The symbol classes are weight-independent unital algebras, yielding limits for finite Toeplitz products and commutators; quantitative Hölder estimates also give finite-rank approximation bounds. The Gaussian case transfers to anti-Wick quantization by unitary equivalence. On compact Kähler manifolds with positive line bundles, we prove a Hölder sufficient condition, including the endpoint, for each fixed bounded second symbol. A projective-line example shows that trace norm convergence can fail for a smooth first symbol and a fixed bounded second symbol. The proofs combine local holomorphic approximation, Schatten and Sobolev estimates, singular integral methods, and the Dunford--Pettis criterion.

papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.authors: Adam Lee; Mutian Xu; Yukang Cao; Shulin Tian; Ziwei Liu
papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history.   Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.

papers.title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography
papers.authors: Yiming Zhang; Jiarui Guo; Haojia Wei; Yifei Liu; Yifan Yang et al.
papers.abstract: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.

papers.title: A flat geodesic with a periodic asymptote
papers.authors: Hongda Qiu
papers.abstract: We construct a closed surface of genus $2$ with nonpositive Gaussian curvature and a complete nonperiodic flat geodesic asymptotic to a flat closed geodesic. The metric is of class $C^{3,1/3}$ and its curvature is of class $C^{1,1/3}$, but not $C^2$. Thus the periodic-asymptote obstruction for smooth surfaces does not extend to $C^1$ Gaussian curvature.

papers.title: Whole-space eventual log-concavity and level-set geometry for the multidimensional Fisher-KPP equation
papers.authors: Xing Liang; Ziqi Zhen
papers.abstract: We study eventual strict log-concavity and level-set geometry for the multidimensional Fisher-KPP equation with nontrivial, nonnegative, smooth compactly supported initial data, without assuming radial symmetry or convexity of the initial superlevel sets. Our main result is that there exist $T>1$ and $c>0$ such that $D_x^2\log u(t,x)\le -(c/t)e^{-β_*t}\mathrm{Id}$ for all $t\ge T$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, where $β_*=2(\sqrt2-1)$. Consequently, after a single waiting time, $u(t,\cdot)$ has exactly one critical point, a nondegenerate global maximizer, and every level set $\{u(t,\cdot)=λ\}$ with $0<λ<\max_x u(t,x)$ is a smooth closed strictly convex hypersurface with positive principal curvatures. For levels in any fixed closed interval $K\subset(0,1)$, the level sets are radial graphs $ρ=R_λ(t,ω)$, with every principal curvature bounded below by $(1-C\log t/t)/(2t)$ for all sufficiently large $t$. Unlike log-concavity, ordinary concavity exhibits a threshold determined by the inflection level of the critical travelling wave: for each fixed level above it, $u$ is eventually strictly concave on its superlevel set, whereas below it concavity eventually fails. Our proof proceeds by establishing estimates in four overlapping spatial regions. In the fixed-front region, we combine a one-sided estimate for second angular derivatives with radial and mixed derivative bounds to obtain curvature control without differentiating the Lipschitz directional phase. In the remaining regions, absorptive comparison in the invaded interior, leading-edge barriers and blow-up arguments through the diffusive scale, and Gaussian amplitude estimates combined with parabolic regularity in the exterior yield the required logarithmic-Hessian bounds.

papers.title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
papers.authors: Jingsong Bai; Ayush Pandey
papers.abstract: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

papers.title: AgentDreamer: Agentic 3D Motion Reasoning for Text-Controllable Physics Simulation
papers.authors: Mijeong Kim; Suho Park; Junha Park; Bohyung Han
papers.abstract: We propose AgentDreamer, an agent-guided optimization framework that aligns text instructions with simulated motion through explicit 3D motion planning. Given a text instruction and scene geometry, an off-the-shelf agent translates the instruction into a structured semantic motion prior, specifying what should move, in which direction, and in what temporal order. The agent represents this prior using parametric functions over a series of temporal chunks, yielding dense 3D trajectories. We then optimize the parameters of a differentiable MPM simulator such that its rollout best matches the prior while remaining constrained by the scene dynamics. This allows the agent to provide semantic guidance from language, while the simulator grounds it in physically feasible motion. We further introduce Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for text-motion alignment based on masked text recovery. By comparing the likelihood of recovering masked motion-related content with and without the simulated motion, Motion-IG measures the information contributed by the motion beyond that available from the remaining text and scene context. Experiments show that AgentDreamer improves text alignment over video-based guidance, producing simulations that more closely follow the requested physical behavior.

papers.title: Emergent Entropic Forces Drive Inverse and Reentrant Phase Transitions in Condensates of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
papers.authors: David A. Herrera-Martí; Marc Jamin
papers.abstract: We present a phenomenological, mean-field model for condensates of intrinsically disordered proteins that describes inverse phase transitions and qualitatively predicts reentrant phase behavior as a function of salt concentration. The model is based on a matrix-based formulation of the Flory-Huggins free energy, in which the enthalpic interaction parameter and the protein valence, defined here as the number of effective "sticky patches", are treated as free parameters. Its central insight is that integrating out dynamics of fast-moving molecular species generates an effective entropic force that increases the free-energy barrier to mixing, even within a mean-field description. We account for this by linking Gaussian integration of co-solutes to the Schur complement of the matrix-based Flory-Huggins free energy. This provides a general thermodynamic framework illustrating how enthalpic interactions that increase the number of available microstates necessarily induce effective entropic forces. We demonstrate the expressiveness and predictive power of the model by qualitatively reproducing recent experimental observations on the rabies virus phosphoprotein.

papers.title: Sharp convergence rate of the estimation error of LASSO via the Feature Space Decomposition method
papers.authors: Guillaume Lecué; Zong Shang
papers.abstract: In this paper, we use the Feature Space Decomposition (FSD) method to establish an explicit, non-asymptotic, instance-optimal convergence rate for the estimation error of the LASSO in the Gaussian linear regression problem for any signal, any diagonal covariance and any regularization parameter above $σ_ξ/\sqrt{N}$ where $σ_ξ$ is the noise variance and $N$ the number of data.

papers.title: GSHeadRelight: Fast Relightability for 3D Gaussian Head Synthesis
papers.authors: Henglei Lv; Bailin Deng; Jianzhu Guo; Xiaoqiang Liu; Pengfei Wan et al.
papers.abstract: Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits are essential in applications such as portrait photography, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). Despite recent progress, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains challenging due to the demands for photorealistic rendering, real-time performance, and generalization to unseen subjects. Existing works either rely on supervision from limited and expensive light stage captured data or produce suboptimal results. Moreover, many works are based on generative NeRFs, which suffer from poor 3D consistency and low real-time performance. We resort to recent progress on generative 3D Gaussians and design a lighting model based on a unified neural radiance transfer representation, which responds linearly to incident light. Using only in-the-wild images, our method achieves state-of-the-art relighting results and a significantly faster rendering speed ($\times12$) compared to previous 3D-aware portrait relighting research. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/GSHeadRelight/.

papers.title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
papers.authors: Kaiyao Liao; Qingfeng Li; Xinlei Zhang; Chen Chen; Qing Sun et al.
papers.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.

papers.title: Detection of Solar-like Oscillations and Granulation at Infrared Wavelengths using JWST
papers.authors: Angharad Weeks; Daniel Huber; Timothy R. Bedding; Jared Splinter; Hans Kjeldsen et al.
papers.abstract: Stellar oscillations and granulation are key probes of stellar convection, one of the most poorly understood processes in stars. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation, but hitherto both processes have only been measured at optical wavelengths. Here we present the first detection of oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 that were obtained to study the atmosphere of an exoplanet. We find that the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but with a functional form that deviates from simple blackbody scaling. The detection opens the door to detailed tests of 3D convection models, facilitates the combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands for exoplanet observations, and supports the predicted asteroseismic yields from the infrared time-domain data that will soon be obtained by the Roman Space Telescope.

papers.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
papers.authors: Rujun Han; Yufan Zhuang; Arijit Ray; Han Yu; Zoey CuiZhu et al.
papers.abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.

papers.title: Localized Neutrinos in Two Dark Dimensions
papers.authors: Waqas Ahmed; George K. Leontaris
papers.abstract: We study neutrino masses in a six-dimensional framework with two compact dark dimensions. In the conventional flat-bulk realization, the sterile-neutrino zero mode is strongly volume suppressed, so a fundamental scale near $10~\mathrm{TeV}$ requires a large higher-dimensional Yukawa coupling to reproduce the observed neutrino masses, while the accompanying two-dimensional Kaluza--Klein tower is strongly constrained by oscillation data. We show that localizing the sterile-neutrino wave function near the Standard-Model brane substantially alleviates both effects. Using a Gaussian localizer, realistic Dirac neutrino masses are obtained with perturbative, order-one Yukawa couplings, while the brane-visible sterile excitations form a shell spectrum with $M_s^2=8μ^2 s$, and squared active--sterile mixings that decrease as $1/s$. The localization scale therefore separates the experimentally relevant sterile-neutrino spectrum from the gravitational compactification scale. We derive the resulting three-flavour structure and study its phenomenological consequences for reactor oscillations and tritium beta decay, including comparisons with current flat-LED and KATRIN constraints.

papers.title: Unified Trajectory and 3D Pose Forecasting for Multi-Agent Sports Analysis
papers.authors: Marc Peral; Guillem Capellera; Luis Ferraz; Antonio Rubio; Stella Graßhof et al.
papers.abstract: Forecasting future human motion requires jointly reasoning about an agent's global trajectory and 3D body pose, which are tightly coupled, particularly in team sports where multiple interacting players introduce complex social dynamics. We exploit a socio-temporal encoder that fuses trajectory and pose at the input level and models them jointly through shared factorized attention. The model is further enhanced by a per-joint loss reweighting scheme that emphasizes dynamic joints and prevents degenerate solutions, and a frequency-domain trajectory smoothing term that improves trajectory prediction while indirectly benefiting pose forecasting. To ensure fair comparison with prior joint forecasting methods, we identify and correct evaluation biases arising from overlapping sequence construction, adopting instead a non-overlapping protocol and a deterministic, oracle-free strategy for multi-future prediction. Our approach improves over prior joint forecasting methods on both WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains on pose accuracy, demonstrating that the proposed joint formulation generalizes beyond the densely interactive scenarios that motivate it.

papers.title: An F-Type Normal-Reference Calibration for High-Dimensional Covariance Testing
papers.authors: Pengfei Wang
papers.abstract: An F-type normal-reference calibration is developed for testing equality of two high-dimensional covariance matrices with unknown means. The test statistic is a ratio whose numerator measures the Frobenius covariance discrepancy and whose denominator estimates its null expectation. Their difference is the complete Li-Chen statistic. Under suitable moment and trace conditions, we establish a Gaussian-reference approximation. After standardization, the statistic and its reference share the normal or nonnormal limits determined by a convergent normalized spectrum. The reference is a ratio of independent chi-square-type mixtures. Applying Welch-Satterthwaite matching to its two components gives an ordinary F approximation, with degrees of freedom estimated from independent four-observation blocks. The effect of estimating the population means is controlled by an exact expansion, and local-power and consistency results are established. The ordinary F approximation is asymptotically valid under a diffuse spectrum, whereas a covariance spike can produce a nonvanishing approximation error. Simulation studies examine empirical size and power under normal and nonnormal sampling. Averaging the trace estimates over fixed partitions improves their stability, but does not remove size inflation in the strongly correlated settings.

papers.title: Optimal Multitask Representations Under a Rate Constraint: An Information Bottleneck Analysis
papers.authors: Nicholas Stiles; Gregory W. Wornell
papers.abstract: Which pretraining objective yields the best representation for downstream tasks under an information budget? We formalize this problem as a multitask information bottleneck, using a mutual information constraint to model incomplete information retention. For Gaussian inputs and tasks, we characterize optimal representations and show that a weakly task-aligned specialist can outperform a reconstruction generalist at low rates but lose at high rates. We also construct task families for which every fixed Gaussian prediction objective incurs arbitrarily large relative regret, driven by reversals in optimal allocation priorities. Conversely, the average task information matrix defines an objective with a uniform relative-regret bound controlled by maximum task SNR. CelebA and dSprites experiments illustrate that compression can change which pretraining objective performs best, and even task-aware training can reverse which downstream task is better preserved as rate increases.

papers.title: Comb Tensor Network Finite-Difference Time-Domain Algorithms for 2D and 3D Electromagnetic Simulations
papers.authors: Jonathan Tabares; Erika Ye; Yang Liu
papers.abstract: This paper presents efficient 2D and 3D finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) algorithms augmented by the comb tensor network (CTN) representation of the field and auxiliary quantities. The proposed CTN-FDTD algorithm leverages superior compressibility of CTN compared with quantized tensor train (QTT), and rank-reduction strategies including local and global smoothing techniques to achieve logarithmic memory requirement and computation (per time step) cost. Numerical examples validate these complexities and demonstrate the applicability of CTN-FDTD using a variety of source excitation, frequency and permittivity profiles in both 2D and 3D. Remarkably, CTN-FDTD can simulate 35 trillion spatial grid points in 3D with low memory and computation costs on one computation node, whereas standard FDTD would require 281 TB memory to store each of its 31 3D arrays. Moreover, CTN-FDTD was applied to realistic 2D photonic crystal structure simulation with one million grid points and 3D scattering analysis with 8.6 billion grid points.

papers.title: Conformal geodesics and the hyperboloid at timelike infinity
papers.authors: Achilleas V. Koukas; Mariem Magdy; Juan A. Valiente Kroon
papers.abstract: A description of scattering in asymptotically flat spacetimes that includes both radiation and massive asymptotic states requires control of the relation between null and timelike infinity. Motivated by this problem, we use the properties of conformal geodesics to construct an extended representation of timelike infinity in Minkowski spacetime. The construction exploits the fact that every non-null metric geodesic in an Einstein spacetime is, up to an explicit local reparametrisation, a conformal geodesic. It replaces the point $i^+$ by a hyperboloidal boundary $\mathcal{H}^+$ meeting future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^+$ at a corner $\mathcal{C}^{+}$, while fixing the location of $\mathscr{I}^+$ in the associated conformal Gaussian gauge. In this gauge, we derive the equations governing massless scalar and spin-$2$ fields. In particular, we obtain a transport equation for the scalar field along future null infinity and analyse the asymptotic behaviour of its spherical-harmonic modes near timelike infinity. We also derive the explicit massless spin-$2$ equations in this gauge. Finally, we examine the relation to projective extensions and to the hyperbolic base of the extended Carrollian space $\mathrm{Ti}$. Our results provide a geometric framework for studying the connection between late-time and null asymptotics which is a prerequisite for scattering constructions relevant to flat space holography.

papers.title: Thermomagnetic enhancement of conserved-charge correlations in a lattice-constrained PNJL model
papers.authors: Bruno S. Lopes; Arthur E. B. Pasqualotto; Jandir J. Buttenbender Filho; Dyana C. Duarte; Ricardo L. S. Farias
papers.abstract: Conserved-charge correlations offer a promising probe of magnetic fields in strongly interacting matter. We investigate their magnetic response and the finite-density equation of state within a lattice-constrained three-flavor Polyakov--Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model. A thermomagnetic scalar coupling, inferred by Gaussian process regression from lattice QCD results for the average light-quark condensate, incorporates inverse magnetic catalysis into the effective interaction. Without fitting conserved-charge observables, the resulting framework substantially improves their magnetic-field dependence and crossover behavior compared with the fixed-coupling model. In particular, it captures the pronounced magnetic enhancement of the baryon--electric-charge correlation and related susceptibility ratios, supporting their use as QCD magnetometers. The comparison demonstrates that the medium dependence of the effective interaction is essential to describe this response within the model. We further calculate pressure Taylor coefficients through sixth order and reconstruct the pressure and baryon density at nonzero baryon chemical potential. Our results show that lattice information from a single chiral observable constrains a broad thermodynamic response, connecting inverse magnetic catalysis, conserved-charge correlations, and the equation of state in a common framework. This provides a lattice-constrained basis for investigating magnetic-field signatures and finite-density thermodynamics in QCD matter.

papers.title: Robust topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff--Love shells by the Speed Method
papers.authors: Philipp Eisenhardt; Fernando Hübner Scherer; Barbara Wohlmuth; Andrei Constantinescu
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for robust topology optimization of Kirchhoff-Love (KL) multi-patch shells using isogeometric analysis and non-matching meshes and provides a CAD-compatible method. The material distribution is optimized via a NURBS-based level set method, enabling accurate boundary representation and seamless export to standard CAD/CAM workflows. The shape derivative is computed using the speed method, yielding a volume-based formulation that avoids boundary approximations and aligns with the isogeometric principle of coarse, high-order discretizations. This eliminates the need for local refinement, adaptive quadrature, or trimming as the descent direction for the compliance and volume objectives are obtained through a biharmonic equation. The framework is extended to robust optimization under uncertainty, accounting for stochastic loading and material properties via Monte Carlo sampling and Gaussian Random Fields. Numerical examples demonstrate the method's efficiency and robustness across single- and multi-patch shells, reproducing literature results with fewer elements than traditional FEM or refined IGA approaches. The developed methods and tools can be directly extended to problems involving stress-based optimization and risk-averse metrics. The numerical implementations are open-source and available on GitHub.

papers.title: Bayesian Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with Abstention
papers.authors: Yuqi Huang; Yunlong Hou; Vincent Y. F. Tan
papers.abstract: We study the Bayesian fixed-confidence best-arm identification problem in which a learner can abstain from making a terminal recommendation. Subject to a target error probability $δ$ and an abstention budget $α$, we propose Screen-and-Confirm (S&C) and analyze its expected stopping time. We further derive the minimum expected stopping time for any algorithm that satisfies these constraints. For Gaussian priors and rewards, as $(δ,α)\downarrow(0,0)$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants, with rate $κ_ν^2[1+\log((α+δ)/δ)]/(α+δ)$, where $κ_ν$ is the prior density of the top-two gap at zero, highlighting that nearly tied instances govern the sampling cost. When abstention is disallowed ($α=0$), S&C yields the optimal $Θ(1/δ)$ dependence for fixed model parameters, removing the additional $\log(1/δ)$ factor in the upper bound of Jang et al. (2024) under our Gaussian assumptions. We further characterize the exact multiplicative constant of the minimum expected stopping time for practical regimes including (i) fixed $α\in (0,1)$ and (ii) $α/δ\to\infty$, which are also achieved by S&C.

papers.title: On the Adversarial Vulnerability of Neural Receivers with Unrolled LDPC Decoders
papers.authors: Aakash Saini; Jafar Aco Mohammadi; Wolfgang Gerstacker
papers.abstract: Neural receivers for 5G New Radio (NR) match classical model-based receivers in link-level performance, but their robustness to adversarial perturbations at the receiver input remains underexplored. We show that standard gradient-based attacks applied end-to-end through an unrolled low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder fail to significantly outperform a matched-power Gaussian perturbation. We identify the failure as gradient masking caused by tanh saturation in the boxplus operation of the belief-propagation (BP) check-node update, with a per-iteration gradient norm decay of more than four orders of magnitude across ten unrolled BP iterations. Based on this finding, we propose two structurally independent loss functions that restore attack efficacy. L_BP routes the gradient through the unsaturated early iterations via per-iteration supervision, while L_LLR is a margin loss on pre-decoder log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) whose gradient bypasses the LDPC decoder entirely. Both loss functions increase the block-error rate (BLER) by one to four orders of magnitude at matched perturbation power, with the results reproduced on both the Sionna NeuralReceiver and DeepRx. At low PSR, L_LLR-optimized perturbations achieve up to three orders of magnitude higher BLER on unseen channel realizations than LBP-optimized perturbations.

papers.title: Foundation4D: Towards a unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles
papers.authors: NVIDIA;  :; Sérgio Agostinho; Maximilian Apodaca; Emmanuel Attia et al.
papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.

papers.title: MoRE: Motion-Regularized Encoding for Articulated 3D Generation
papers.authors: Guantian Zheng; Shan Jin
papers.abstract: Generating an articulated object from a single image requires recovering both its appearance and the mechanism governing its parts. A compact encoding of joint attributes does not by itself ensure that reconstruction preserves the resulting motion. We present MoRE, Motion-Regularized Encoding for articulated 3D generation. MoRE represents coordinate-aligned joint lines with axis classification and two axis-orthogonal Plücker moment coefficients, removing the arbitrary choice of an origin along the axis. During representation learning, decoded joint hypotheses are used to move corresponding three-dimensional anchors, and their motions are compared with those of annotated joints. A differentiable expectation over joint types and axis directions couples attribute reconstruction to the motion it induces. An image-conditioned flow learns the resulting functional latents, while a multi-state-adapted Gaussian model supplies appearance. At inference, recovered part assignments and joints articulate a single set of rest-pose Gaussians without regenerating the object for each state. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility and ACD show stronger part-box agreement, articulated-state geometry and visual similarity than the compared baselines, while joint prediction reduces axis, origin and range errors relative to ArtiLatent. Controlled ablations support the joint-line encoding and show that motion supervision reduces anchor-motion error. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be released in the future.

papers.title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Bangpu Chen; Yaxuan Li; Shirui Peng; Xiangtian Si; Liuxin Chu et al.
papers.abstract: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.

papers.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
papers.authors: Zikang Xiong; Weixin Li; Zhouchonghao Wu; Akshay Rangesh; Saarth Bonde et al.
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.

papers.title: SciFusion: Physics-Guided Compositional Diffusion for Multimodal 3D Scientific Image Generation
papers.authors: Luoxi Wang; Alessio Quercia; Hanno Scharr; Arya Bangun
papers.abstract: Existing 3D generative approaches are typically developed for individual imaging modalities, requiring substantial modality-specific data and limiting their ability to exploit shared structure across scientific imaging domains. We present SciFusion, a multimodal framework for unified 3D scientific image generation built on a latent diffusion backbone, with two key contributions. First, we introduce a compositional conditioning scheme that factorizes each modality into domain, object, and contrast representations. Sharing these factors across related modalities enables knowledge transfer across heterogeneous imaging domains and allows the factors to be recombined at inference time to synthesize unseen domain-object-contrast compositions in a zero-shot manner. Second, we incorporate domain-specific physics-informed objectives: Fourier spectral consistency for MRI, Radon projection consistency for CT, and multislice diffraction consistency for electron microscopy, to encourage generated samples to respect modality-dependent image formation processes. Extensive experiments across 15 medical and scientific imaging modalities demonstrate that SciFusion improves generation fidelity and cross-domain generalization over modality-specific and flattened multimodal conditioning strategies, while enabling zero-shot synthesis of unseen compositions without training on those target compositions. These results demonstrate that compositional, physics-guided conditioning provides a scalable framework for unified 3D scientific image generation, particularly for emerging modalities where large-scale training data are difficult to obtain.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Dimension Reduction and Surrogates for Partially Linear Bayesian Inverse Problems
papers.authors: Ziheng Zhang; Dingcheng Luo; Thomas O'Leary-Roseberry; Umberto Villa; Omar Ghattas
papers.abstract: Many Bayesian inverse problems are characterized by two parameter vectors with distinct roles. A medium property, operator coefficient, or geometry block enters the forward model nonlinearly, whereas a volumetric, initial condition, or boundary condition source enters linearly. General-purpose nonlinear surrogates must relearn this known source dependence from data and may not preserve the correct source scaling outside the training regime. We introduce a structure-preserving partially linear (SPPL) framework that constructs separate reduced spaces for outputs, (linearly appearing) sources, and (nonlinearly appearing) medium variables and represents the reduced forward map as an affine function of the retained source coordinates, with coefficients that depend on the medium variables. Here, "affine" refers to the retained, mean-centered source coordinates: the physical forward map remains linear in the source, while the affine offset is induced by the source-prior mean and vanishes when that mean is zero. The analysis first identifies the optimal blockwise ridge approximation and then derives the optimal affine-in-source approximation under independent medium and source priors.
